title: z-test
summary: A z-test of a mean uses the statistic (x̄ − μ0) divided by σ over square root n, with σ known or with a stated large-sample approximation. Rejection regions depend on whether the alternative is one-sided or two-sided. The p-value is computed under the null.
intuition:
A z-test asks whether a sample mean is far from a hypothesised value $\mu_0$, on the scale of the standard error. The primary statistic, when $\sigma$ is known, is

$$
z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Under the null hypothesis $\mu=\mu_0$, and with normal data or a large-sample approximation, this statistic is compared with a standard normal reference. If $\sigma$ is unknown, the exact normal-data test is the t-test. Replacing $\sigma$ by $s$ and still using normal critical values is a stated large-sample approximation, not the small-sample procedure.

The rejection region follows the alternative. An upper one-sided test of $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ rejects for large positive $z$, at 5% when $z>z_{0.05}=1.645$. A lower one-sided test rejects for large negative $z$. A two-sided test of $H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0$ rejects when $|z|>z_{0.025}=1.96$ at the 5% level, and when $|z|>z_{0.005}=2.576$ at the 1% level. A statistic that is large and positive is evidence against the null in the upper tail. It is not evidence for a lower-tailed alternative.

The p-value is computed under the null. It is the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction the alternative calls extreme. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value says the data are awkward for the null. It does not say how probable the null is.

definitions.body: With known $\sigma$, $z=(\bar x-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$. The null value $\mu_0$ is what the hypothesis fixes, not the sample mean.
At level 5%, an upper one-sided test rejects when $z>1.645$, and a two-sided test rejects when $|z|>1.96$. The lower one-sided region is $z<-1.645$.
The p-value is a probability computed under $H_0$: the chance of a result at least as extreme as the observed statistic. It is not $P(H_0\text{ is true})$.
If $\sigma$ is replaced by $s$ and the statistic is still referred to the standard normal, that is a large-sample approximation. The exact test for normal data with unknown $\sigma$ is the t-test.

formulas.name: Statistic
formulas.note: Known $\sigma$. A large-sample version may state that $s$ replaces $\sigma$.

formulas.name: Two-sided 5% rejection
formulas.note: Upper one-sided 5% rejection is $z>1.645$. Two-sided 1% rejection is $|z|>2.576$.

properties: The z statistic for a mean is $(\bar x-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$ when $\sigma$ is known. The reference distribution under $H_0$ is standard normal, for normal data or as a stated large-sample approximation.
An upper one-sided 5% test rejects when $z>1.645$. A two-sided 5% test rejects when $|z|>1.96$. A two-sided 1% test rejects when $|z|>2.576$.
The p-value is computed assuming $H_0$ is true. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and it is not the probability that $H_1$ is true.
The direction matters. A positive statistic is in the rejection region of an upper one-sided test and in the wrong tail of a lower one-sided test.
Replacing $\sigma$ by $s$ inside a z statistic is a large-sample approximation. For normal data and an estimated scale, the matching test is the t-test with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

examples.title: A two-sided test with known σ
examples.prompt: Test $H_0:\mu=50$ against a two-sided alternative. The sample size is $n=25$, $\sigma=10$ is known, and $\bar x=56$.
steps: The standard error is $10/\sqrt{25}=2$. The statistic is $(56-50)/2=3$.
The two-sided 5% test rejects when $|z|>1.96$. Since $3>1.96$, the test rejects $H_0$ at 5%.

The two-sided 1% test rejects when $|z|>2.576$. Since $3>2.576$, it also rejects at 1%. The two-sided p-value is $2(1-\Phi(3))$, a probability computed under $H_0$. It is not the probability that $\mu$ equals 50.
examples.answer: The statistic is $z=3$. The two-sided test rejects $H_0$ at both 5% and 1%.

examples.title: The same statistic, two different alternatives
examples.prompt: A sample of size $n=100$ has $\sigma=5$ known and $\bar x=11$. Test $H_0:\mu=10$, first against $H_1:\mu<10$ and then against $H_1:\mu>10$, at the 5% level.
steps: The standard error is $5/10=0.5$. The statistic is $(11-10)/0.5=2$.
The lower one-sided 5% rejection region is $z<-1.645$. The observed value 2 is in the wrong tail, so the lower-tailed test does not reject.

The upper one-sided 5% rejection region is $z>1.645$. Since $2>1.645$, the upper-tailed test rejects. The number 2 is also larger than 1.96, so a two-sided 5% test would reject, but it is smaller than 2.576, so a two-sided 1% test would not.
examples.answer: The statistic is $z=2$. The lower-tailed 5% test does not reject. The upper-tailed 5% test does.

traps: Calling the p-value the probability that $H_0$ is true. The p-value is computed under the null. It is a tail probability for the statistic, not a posterior probability of the hypothesis.
Using a two-sided critical value on a one-sided test, or the reverse. At 5%, the one-sided normal critical value is 1.645 and the two-sided critical value is 1.96.
Rejecting a lower-tailed alternative because $z$ is large and positive. The sign has to match the alternative. A positive statistic is the wrong tail for $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$.
Treating a z-test with an estimated $s$ as exact for a small normal sample. That is a large-sample approximation. The exact normal-data procedure with unknown $\sigma$ is the t-test.

questions.stem: Test $H_0:\mu=20$ with $n=16$, known $\sigma=4$, and $\bar x=23$. The z statistic is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $3$.

The standard error is $4/\sqrt{16}=1$, so $z=(23-20)/1=3$. Option B divides the difference 3 by $\sigma=4$ and forgets $\sqrt{n}$. Option D divides by $2$. Option C multiplies the difference by $\sigma$. The statistic uses the known $\sigma$. It is not a t statistic.

questions.stem: A z-test of $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ reports a p-value of 0.03. That p-value is
options: the probability, under $H_0$, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed
always equal to the probability that a 95% interval misses $\mu_0$
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

A p-value is computed under the null hypothesis. It is the tail probability of the test statistic, with the tail chosen by the alternative. It is not $P(H_0\text{ is true})$ and it is not $P(H_1\text{ is true})$. Option D confuses a p-value with the coverage error of a confidence procedure. Those are related ideas and they are not the definition of the number 0.03.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of a z-test for a mean?
options: When $\sigma$ is known, the statistic is $(\bar x-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$.
An upper one-sided 5% test rejects when $z>1.645$.
The p-value equals the probability that $H_0$ is true.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The statistic uses the known scale $\sigma$ and the null value $\mu_0$. The 5% critical values are 1.96 for a two-sided test and 1.645 for an upper one-sided test. Option D is the standard misreading. The p-value is computed under $H_0$. It is not $P(H_0\text{ is true}\mid \text{data})$.

questions.stem: A test of $H_0:\mu=10$ uses $n=100$, known $\sigma=5$, and $\bar x=11$, so the z statistic equals 2. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A and C**.

The standard error is $5/\sqrt{100}=0.5$ and $z=(11-10)/0.5=2$. An upper 5% test rejects because $2>1.645$. A two-sided 5% test rejects because $2>1.96$. A lower 5% test rejects only for $z<-1.645$, so B is false. A two-sided 1% test rejects only for $|z|>2.576$, and $2<2.576$, so D is false.

questions.stem: A z-test uses known $\sigma=9$, sample size $n=36$, and $\bar x-\mu_0=6$. Enter the z statistic.
questions.solution:
The answer is **4**.

The standard error is $9/\sqrt{36}=9/6=1.5$. The statistic is $6/1.5=4$. The comparison with 1.96 or 1.645 is a later step. The question asks for the statistic itself, and the arithmetic uses the known $\sigma$.
